title: The Year of the Elephant
subtitle: Before his birth, the world already bowed to his coming
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the opening of the biography
Qur'an 105 (Surah Al-Fil) — the armies of the elephant

chapters.heading: Abraha's Army and the Falling Birds
chapters.body: In the year the Prophet ﷺ was born, Abraha al-Ashram, the Christian ruler of Yemen, built a magnificent cathedral in Sana'a — and then marched on Makkah with elephants to pull the Arabs away from the Kaaba to his new shrine. The Qur'an compressed that arrogance into five verses: 'Have you not considered, [O Muhammad], how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, Striking them with stones of hard clay, And He made them like eaten straw' (105:1-5). The seerah of Ibn Ishaq records what the Arabs called that year forever after: the Year of the Elephant — the year the Kabah humbled an empire, in the year the boy was born (the date is a seerah report) who would make that humble House the qiblah of the world. From his first breath, history arranged itself around him.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Allah defended His House with birds. What big threat in your life might look smaller if you remembered Who is defending you?

title: The Orphan of Makkah
subtitle: Amina's son, Halimah's milk, Abu Talib's shadow
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the fosterage and the opening years
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — Halimah's account of the fosterage (not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)

chapters.heading: The Child Who Brought Blessing
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, son of Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb. His father died before his birth, and by desert custom he was given to a foster mother of Banu Sa'd — and the seerah records that Halimah's household, poor and dry, blossomed the moment she took him: her flock fattened, her milk flowed, and she pressed to keep the child an extra season (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; not from the six books). At six, his mother Amina died on the road home from Madinah at a place called Abwa, and the boy came back to Makkah an orphan twice over. His grandfather Abdul-Muttalib took him in and adored him — keeping the child beside him in the council of Quraysh where no child had ever sat — and when the old man died, Muhammad ﷺ passed to his uncle Abu Talib, who guarded him for forty years. The Qur'an would one day name his condition over him: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge?' (93:6). Orphanhood was his first teacher; protection was his Lord's first gift.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ lost his parents as a small child and was still raised with love. Who shelters the vulnerable people around you — and could that be you?

title: Al-Amin, The Trustworthy
subtitle: The honest young man the Quraysh could not bribe
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the merchant of Khadijah and the rebuilding of the Kaaba
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Khadijah's testimony to his character

chapters.heading: The Merchant of Makkah
chapters.body: As a young man, Muhammad ﷺ entered the caravan trade, and the seerah records that the merchants learned to trust him above their own accountants — so much that the wealthy Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, hearing of his honesty, sent him her capital to trade in Syria with her servant Maysarah. The journey returned double its profit and Maysarah returned with a story: two angels had shaded him from the sun. Khadijah proposed marriage through a friend, and though she was fifteen years his senior and the nobles of Makkah had sought her, she chose the orphan of Abu Talib. Years later, when revelation first shook him, her answer named the character of his whole youth: 'You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). Makkah's nickname for him before any revelation was simple: Al-Amin — the Trustworthy.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Khadijah listed five habits that proved his prophethood. Which of the five — kin, the weak, guests, hardship, truth — needs your work this month?

title: The Cave of Hira
subtitle: Forty years of silence before the first word
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the retreat to Hira
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Aisha's narration of the first revelation
Qur'an 96:1-5 — the first revealed words

chapters.heading: Solitude Before the Storm
chapters.body: In his late thirties, Muhammad ﷺ began leaving Makkah's noise for the cave of Hira on Jabal an-Nur, taking provisions and turning his face to the silence. The seerah records that he would stay days at a time in the cave, thinking — a man of Makkah withdrawing from Makkah, troubled by the idols he had never bowed to. In the month of Ramadan, in the year he turned forty, the silence ended. The angel came to him and said: Iqra — Read. He answered: I am not one who can read. The angel embraced him until it was more than he could bear, then released him and repeated the command — three times — until the words descended: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Created man from a clinging substance. Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous - Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). The first word of the final revelation was not a command to rule or to fight. It was a command to read, in the name of the One who created — and the first description of the Lord it gave was not power, but generosity (96:3).

chapters.heading: Khadijah's Test
chapters.body: He ran home from the cave trembling, asking to be covered, and told Khadijah what he had seen — and her response, preserved in Bukhari's Sahih, became the first theology of the new religion: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Bukhari 3). Notice: his wife reasoned from character to truth. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar, who heard the description and said the words that confirmed everything: 'This is the same one who keeps the secrets whom Allah had sent to Moses' (Bukhari 3). The first consultant of the prophethood was a woman; the first confirmation came from a Christian scholar who knew the scriptures. From its first hour, this message crossed every boundary people build.

familyQuestion: The first command of the final revelation was Iqra — Read. What is your relationship with reading — and could one good book change your family's next year?

title: Three Years of Whispers
subtitle: The secret call — the first believers
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the private preaching
Qur'an 26:214 — 'warn, [O Muhammad], your closest kindred'
Musnad Ahmad — Ali's account of the meal for Banu Hashim (number not verified; Disputed in the sources)

chapters.heading: The Call and the Feast
chapters.body: For three years the call moved quietly — from house to house, trusted friend to trusted friend. The seerah reports name Khadijah, Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr among the first to believe (the order is discussed in the sources) — a woman, a youth, a freed slave, a merchant: the future of the ummah in miniature. When the command came — 'warn, [O Muhammad], your closest kindred' (26:214) — Muhammad ﷺ climbed Safa and called the clans of Quraysh, asking them: if I told you horsemen were in this valley, would you believe me? They said: yes, we have never found you but truthful. He said: then I am a warner before a severe punishment (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Abu Lahab cursed him and left — and a verse descended on that day naming the uncle's end (111:1-5). Disputed in the sources — the account of a meal for Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib is reported in Musnad Ahmad (the number was not verified) and its wording is contested: 'Which of you will assist me in this matter, so that he is my brother, my executor, my successor among you?' The room fell silent — and Ali, barely into his teens, stood and said: I will, though I am the youngest. Muhammad ﷺ placed his hand on Ali's neck and said: this is my brother, my successor among you.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The first believers were a woman, a teenager, and a freed slave. What does that tell you about whose hearts Allah chooses first?

title: Bilal and the Heavy Sand
subtitle: The slave who taught the world a word: Ahad
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the persecution of the weak believers
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — Abu Bakr's freeing of Bilal (not from the six books)

chapters.heading: Ahad, Ahad
chapters.body: When the call went public and Quraysh could not bribe or debate it down, they turned to the believers who had no tribe to shield them. Bilal ibn Rabah, the Abyssinian slave, was dragged at noon onto the burning sand of Makkah, a boulder pressed on his chest, and told to renounce — and his answer, seared into every generation since, was one word: Ahad — One. One God. Umayyah ibn Khalaf tortured him past the limits of endurance, and the seerah reports say Abu Bakr bought him and freed him (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; source not checked here; not from the six books). The men with nothing became the carriers of everything: Bilal, Ammar, Sumayyah, Suhayb, Khabbab — the weak of Makkah out-argued its chiefs and out-suffered its torturers, and the truth did not need the strong to survive. It needed the sincere.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Bilal had one word under a boulder: Ahad. If your faith cost you comfort today, what would your one word be?

title: The Night of the Journey
subtitle: Al-Isra wal-Mi'raj — five prayers as the gift of the heavens
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 — the full narration of the Night Journey
Qur'an 17:1 — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night'
Sahih Muslim 162 — the fifty prayers reduced to five

chapters.heading: From the Haram to the Farthest Mosque
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ was carried from the sacred mosque to the farthest mosque in a single night: 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed' (17:1). From Jerusalem he ascended through the heavens — Bukhari preserves the narration in full — past Adam at the first heaven, Isa and Yahya, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa, and Ibrahim leaning against the Bayt al-Ma'mur, to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary. Musa asked him at the end what his nation had been given, and when he heard fifty prayers a day, Musa said: your people cannot bear fifty — go back and ask your Lord to lighten it (Bukhari 349, Muslim 162). He returned and returned again, until the covenant stood at five prayers for the reward of fifty — until, in the narration, the word came: they are five, and they are fifty; My word is not changed (Muslim 162). The five daily prayers are not a burden negotiated down. They are a gift negotiated up — from the Lord of the heavens, through the stubborn love of Musa for the believers, to your doorstep five times a day.

familyQuestion: Five prayers were gifted from above the seven heavens. Do you treat them as a burden negotiated down — or a gift you get to keep?

title: The Boycott
subtitle: Three years in the valley — the written siege
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the document of the boycott
Qur'an 111 — 'May the hands of Abu Lahab perish'

chapters.heading: A Document Against a Clan
chapters.body: When persuasion, bribery, and torture failed, Quraysh tried isolation. The clans wrote a document — the seerah records its hanging inside the Kaaba — binding themselves: no marrying the Banu Hashim, no selling to them, no sitting with them, until they surrendered Muhammad ﷺ to be killed. The document turned Makkah into a prison for one clan. For three years the Hashim and al-Muttalib, Muslims and non-Muslims among them alike, ate leaves and the milk of a single she-camel, in the stony valley outside the city. Khadijah's wealth drained away in those years — the seerah historians count the boycott among the causes of her death soon after. And then the tide turned from an unexpected place: some Qurayshis themselves, sickened by watching relatives starve, began passing food secretly; then Hisham ibn Amr and others worked openly until the document — which, the tradition records, termites had devoured except the words 'in Your name, O Allah' — was declared void by the very men who wrote it. A starving clan had outlasted an empire's merchant aristocracy, and the famine broke before the faith did.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The boycott starved the Muslims for three years but broke before their faith did. What pressure are you under that only feels permanent?

title: The First Hijrah
subtitle: Abyssinia — the king whose bishops wept and refused the extradition
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the emigration to Abyssinia
Musnad Ahmad — Ja'far's speech before the Negus (number not verified)

chapters.heading: A Kingdom That Let Them Pray
chapters.body: When the persecution of the weak believers became unbearable, the Prophet ﷺ told the believers: go to Abyssinia — there is a king there under whom no one is wronged. It was the first emigration of the Muslim community: no army, no land promised, just a king they had never met. And when the Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to demand their extradition, the Negus convened his bishops — and the bishops, like professionals everywhere, asked about doctrine before character. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered by reciting from Surah Maryam — and the king and his priests wept until their beards were wet, and the Negus refused the extradition with the sentence history remembers: go, for by Allah, I will never surrender you to them (reported by Ahmad; the number was not verified). A Christian kingdom had become the first refuge of Islam — proof that truth recognizes truth across every border.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Negus protected strangers he had no reason to protect. Have you ever been protected by a stranger — or been one for someone else?

title: The Conversion of Umar
subtitle: The man who set out to kill the Prophet ﷺ became his shield
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the conversion narrative
Sahih al-Bukhari 3680 — the Prophet's ﷺ dream of Umar's palace in Paradise

chapters.heading: A Lion Changes Direction
chapters.body: Umar ibn al-Khattab was the strongest man of Quraysh, and for years he used that strength against Islam — until the day he strapped on his sword and walked to kill Muhammad ﷺ, as he himself narrated. On the road a man told him: begin with your own house — his sister Fatima bint al-Khattab and her husband had embraced the faith. Umar burst in, heard the pages of Surah Ta-Ha being recited, and struck his brother-in-law — and then his sister, when she rose to shield her husband. Blood on her face, she said the sentence no sword in Makkah could survive: 'We have become Muslims, whether you like it or not.' Umar stood still — and asked to see what they were reading. The page was given to him washed clean, and he read, and the man the Quraysh feared most walked to Dar al-Arqam and said the shahada.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Umar's sister spoke truth to a sword and it disarmed him. When did truth spoken gently change you?

title: Taif
subtitle: Stoned at the city gates — and answered with a prayer for their children
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the journey to Taif
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — the Prophet's ﷺ words in the valley

chapters.heading: The Saddest Day of the Seerah
chapters.body: After the Year of Sorrow — the deaths of Khadijah and Abu Talib in the same year — the Prophet ﷺ walked alone to Taif, seventy miles away, to seek protection. The chiefs of Taif refused him, and set the street urchins and slaves to stone him. He fled the city bleeding, and took shelter in a vineyard, and there — with wounds still fresh — he raised his hands: 'O Allah, to You alone I complain of my weakness, my scarcity of resources, and my humiliation before the people... If You are not displeased with me, then I do not care' (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; not from the six books). Then Jibril came with the angel of the mountains, offering to bring the two mountains together upon the city. The Prophet ﷺ answered with the sentence that made Taif's grandchildren his own: 'No — I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone' (Bukhari 3231). The seerah reports say that years later a delegation from Taif came to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam (details not checked here).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The man they stoned prayed for their grandchildren. Is there someone who hurt you whose children you could still bless?

title: The Pledges of Aqabah
subtitle: Seventy-five hands in the dark — Madinah accepts the message
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the first and second pledges
Sahih al-Bukhari 18 — the pledge of Aqabah: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good (narrated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit)

chapters.heading: Twelve, Then Seventy-Five
chapters.body: At the pilgrimage seasons, the Prophet ﷺ met men from Yathrib — a city torn by tribal war, hungry for an arbitrator above tribes. The first year, six believed. The next, twelve men pledged at Aqabah in the dark: no shirk with Allah, no theft, no adultery, no killing of children, no slander, no disobedience in good conduct — the first charter of the Muslim community, taken hand by hand (Sahih al-Bukhari 18). Mus'ab ibn Umair was sent back with them (the seerah reports place this after the first pledge) as Islam's first ambassador — to teach the Qur'an and lead the prayer. The next year, about seventy-five came by night and pledged (seerah reports; the numbers vary in the sources). The Ansar of Madinah were preparing a city before the Prophet ﷺ had ever seen it.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Ansar believed in a man they had met twice. What makes someone trustworthy enough to follow?

title: The Hijrah
subtitle: The cave, the companion, and the man who rode for a bounty
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'as one of two, when they were in the cave' (revealed for this night)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 — the Hijrah with Abu Bakr, including the cave
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the route and the details

chapters.heading: The Second of Two
chapters.body: On the night Quraysh had finally voted to kill him — one man from every clan, so the blood-price would crush Banu Hashim — the Prophet ﷺ slipped out of Makkah with Abu Bakr. At the cave of Thawr, with the hunters at the mouth, Abu Bakr whispered his fear that the hunters might see them. And the Prophet ﷺ answered with the words Allah preserved in the Qur'an: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). Later tradition adds a spider's web and a dove's nest at the entrance; these are not in the Qur'an or in Bukhari 3905 and no chain was verified for this audit. The Qur'an says only that Allah 'supported him with angels you did not see' (9:40). Behind them came Suraqa ibn Malik, riding for a hundred-camel bounty — until his horse sank in the ground, twice, and the third time he called out terms of surrender and asked the Prophet ﷺ to write him a letter of safety. The hunter rode home guarding a document he had come to kill for. The two travelers reached Quba, and then reached Madinah.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Allah sealed the cave with a spider's web — the weakest of guards. What 'weak' thing in your life might actually be Allah's protection?

title: The Arrival in Madinah
subtitle: Every roof emptied, every voice shouting one word: the Messenger has come
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the entry into Madinah

chapters.heading: A City That Ran to Meet Him
chapters.body: At Quba, the Prophet ﷺ spent days building the first masjid of Islam — Masjid Quba, the mosque the Qur'an itself honors: 'a mosque founded on righteousness from the first day' (9:108). Then he rode toward Madinah, and the city emptied onto the roads and the rooftops: men, women, children, everyone calling out in one rising chorus — 'the Messenger of Allah has come!' — until the date palms of Madinah, the tradition says, were crowded with people. He let his camel wander free, saying: let it go its way, for it is guided — and the camel knelt at the courtyard of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, where he stayed as a guest. The Ansar and Muhajirun began pairing themselves brother by brother, and when one Ansari offered to split his palm-trees and his wealth in half, the Prophet ﷺ answered: may Allah bless you in your wealth and your family — keep your money, and show me the market. The first economy of Islam was: work honestly, and family is whoever shares your roof.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Ansar gave strangers half of everything. What would you genuinely share with someone who had nothing?

title: The Charter of Madinah
subtitle: One document, one ummah — many faiths under one covenant
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the text of the Charter (sahifa)

chapters.heading: Writing a Nation
chapters.body: Within the first year, the Prophet ﷺ did something no conqueror does: he sat with the Jewish clans of Madinah and wrote a charter — the Sahifa — making one ummah of the believers and the Jews, each with their religion and their alliances, one hand against any aggressor, disputes referred to Allah and His Messenger. Abdullah ibn Salam, a Jewish scholar of Madinah, embraced Islam in these early days (his own account is in the hadith literature; the number and wording were not re-checked here). For a time, Madinah lived the experiment: one city, many religions, one covenant. The hypocrites — those who said with their mouths what their hearts denied (63:1) — tested it from within, and some clan leaders tested it from without, until the covenant's clauses were broken one by one and its sanctions came due one by one. But the document itself stands in history: a remarkable early written covenant for a plural city, in the reports that preserve it.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Charter made one nation of different faiths. What community are you part of that needs one covenant more than it needs one religion?

title: The Qibla Changes
subtitle: Sixteen months toward Jerusalem — then one command turned a congregation around
sources: Qur'an 2:142-150 — the whole passage, 'We see the turning of your face'
Sahih al-Bukhari 399 — the change of the qiblah

chapters.heading: Turning the Whole Community
chapters.body: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah (Bukhari 399), the Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem — the qiblah of Ibrahim and Musa. Some people were not content with it. And the Prophet ﷺ, who used to face the heavens waiting for the command, received it mid-prayer: a prayer (placing it in a zuhr prayer at the mosque of Banu Salama is a later tradition we have not verified), during which the verse descended — 'So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (2:144) — and the worshippers turned toward Makkah mid-prayer (Bukhari 399). Allah framed the change itself as revelation about revelation: 'We have certainly seen the turning of your face, [O Muhammad], toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased' (2:144) — and then taught the deeper lesson: it is not righteousness to face east or west (2:177). And the fools said, 'What has turned them from their qiblah?' — to which the answer came: 'Say, To Allah belongs the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path' (2:142).

familyQuestion: The whole congregation turned mid-prayer without arguing. When has your community changed direction without splitting?

title: Badr: The Two Armies Meet
subtitle: 313 against a thousand — and Allah was the third of three
sources: Qur'an 3:123-127 — 'already had Allah given you victory at [the battle of] Badr'
Qur'an 8:41 — 'that which We sent down to Our Servant on the day of criterion'

chapters.heading: The Criterion
chapters.body: The Qur'an later named the day: 'if you have believed in Allah and in that which We sent down to Our Servant on the day of criterion - the day when the two armies met' (8:41). About three hundred believers (the seerah reports say 313) faced about a thousand of Quraysh with their full caravan wealth behind them. The Prophet ﷺ spent the night before the battle in prayer under a tree. At dawn, the Prophet ﷺ arranged the ranks with an arrow — and the Qur'an recorded the divine arithmetic of that morning: 'And already had Allah given you victory at [the battle of] Badr while you were few in number' (3:123); and, of the same day, 'so that Allah might accomplish a matter already destined' (8:42). Three thousand angels, it says — 'And Allah made it not except as [a sign of] good tidings for you and to reassure your hearts thereby. And victory is not except from Allah' (3:126).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Allah sent angels but said victory is only from Him. When you win, who do you thank first?

title: Badr: The Prisoners
subtitle: Nobles of Quraysh in chains — and the Prophet's ﷺ mercy toward them
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the treatment of the prisoners
Qur'an 8:67-71 — 'It is not for a prophet to have captives [of war] until he inflicts a massacre [upon Allah 's enemies] in the land'

chapters.heading: Mercy After Victory
chapters.body: The battle broke Quraysh utterly: nobles dead on the field, nobles in chains, the caravan escaped only by Allah's decree. And the Prophet ﷺ did what no Arab war custom allowed — he treated the prisoners kindly, as the seerah reports tell it, and set the ransom of some literate prisoners at teaching Muslim children to read (a report whose source was not checked here). The revelation that descended about the day named the tension honestly: 'It is not for a prophet to have captives [of war] until he inflicts a massacre [upon Allah 's enemies] in the land' (8:67) — the desire for spoils had nearly cost them the mission. But the surah closed on the law that outlasted the battle: 'So consume what you have taken of war booty [as being] lawful and good, and fear Allah' (8:69) — and on the prisoners themselves: 'If Allah knows [any] good in your hearts, He will give you [something] better than what was taken from you' (8:70). The sources name some of those prisoners as later accepting Islam. Victory at Badr was measured not in the dead, but in the converts.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ fed his enemies from his own table. When did mercy after winning cost you nothing but pride?

title: Uhud: The Day the Line Broke
subtitle: Archers leave the pass — and the Prophet ﷺ bleeds on the mountain
sources: Qur'an 3:152-155 — the day 'some of you desired the world'
Qur'an 3:144 — 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4043-4044 — the archers who left their post at Uhud

chapters.heading: The Turning
chapters.body: The archers held the pass behind the Muslims as ordered — until the spoils of the routed enemy appeared, and most of them descended, against orders, for their share. Khalid ibn al-Walid, still an enemy commander that day, saw the pass empty and wheeled his cavalry through it. The Muslim line broke from behind; Hamza, the master of martyrs, fell; and the Prophet ﷺ — wounded in the face, a tooth broken, rumor running the field that he had been killed — stood on the slope with the remnant around him. The verse descended that anchors the whole religion: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger. [Other] messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]?' (3:144). The Muslims rallied to the slope; the Quraysh withdrew. And the revelation's verdict on the day named the lesson every generation inherits: 'And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing the enemy by His permission until [the time] when you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order [given by the Prophet] and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love' (3:152) — victory had come by obedience; its near-loss came by desire. The spoils of Uhud were a Qur'an.

familyQuestion: The archers left their post for spoils and nearly lost everything. What 'post' are you tempted to leave right now?

title: Uhud: Hamza and the Women
subtitle: The master of martyrs, the mutilated dead, and Hind's answer
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — Hamza's death and the aftermath
Qur'an 16:126-128 — 'And if you punish [an enemy, O believers], punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed'

chapters.heading: The Lion and the Lesson
chapters.body: Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib — the uncle who embraced Islam in the early years, called the Lion of Allah in the reports — was killed by an Abyssinian spear for hire, and the seerah records that his body was mutilated on the field, and that the Prophet ﷺ stood by what had been done to his uncle and wept, and said: I will mutilate seventy of them for you — until the revelation descended and forbade it: 'And if you punish [an enemy, O believers], punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed. But if you are patient - it is better for those who are patient' (16:126). And he ﷺ was patient — and the mutilation of the dead was abolished from his law forever, in a century that knew no such mercy. Hind bint Utbah, whom the reports name as behind the mutilation, later became a Muslim (seerah; details not checked here). The law that answered mutilation with patience built an empire; the vengeance that answered it would have built a feud.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ forbade mutilating the dead in a century that knew no such mercy. What revenge habit could your family end with you?

title: The Trench
subtitle: Ten thousand at the walls — and a biting wind from the unseen
sources: Qur'an 33:9-27 — '[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you'
Qur'an 33:10-11 — 'there the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking'
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the digging of the trench

chapters.heading: The Severe Shaking
chapters.body: Madinah had a side the armies could not cross — the lava fields and the palm groves — and the Prophet ﷺ, taking the advice of Salman the Persian, ordered a trench dug along the open quarter. The believers dug through the cold nights, and the hypocrites stood at the edge bargaining: a trench against the horsemen of Quraysh? — 'that is what the Persians do' (Ibn Ishaq). Then the alliance arrived: ten thousand — Quraysh from the south, Ghatafan from the east, with chiefs of the exiled Jewish clan of Banu Nadir having helped to rally them (a seerah report). The Qur'an preserved the city at its breaking point: '[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted [in fear], and hearts reached the throats and you assumed about Allah [various] assumptions. There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking' (33:10-11). And then, at the height of the siege — with the trench holding, with Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud sowing distrust between the allies as a new Muslim working from inside — the wind came: a bitter gale that blew for days, freezing the besiegers in their camps and tearing their tents, until the alliance dissolved and marched away without a battle being fought (33:9). Madinah had not won the Trench. Allah had.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The trench held because Salman, a Persian outsider, was listened to. Whose 'outsider' idea are you ignoring right now?

title: Hudaybiyyah
subtitle: The treaty that looked like defeat — and became the greatest victory
sources: Qur'an 48:1-3 — 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 — the terms of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah
Reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — Umar's objection at Hudaybiyyah (hadith numbers not re-checked in this build)

chapters.heading: The Clear Conquest
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah to perform umrah in peace, about fourteen hundred men in ihram (the reports give about 1,400) — and Quraysh stopped them at Hudaybiyyah. The treaty that followed looked like surrender: return this year, ten years' truce, a Qurayshi who came to Madinah without his guardian's leave would be sent back, while a Muslim who went to Quraysh would not. Umar ibn al-Khattab could not bear it: are we not upon the truth? — until the Prophet ﷺ answered with certainty that has guided statesmen since: I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger; I will not disobey Him, and He will not neglect me (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). And the Qur'an named what no eye could see: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest' (48:1). Within two years the truce had emptied Arabia's idolaters of every excuse: the Muslims preached in peace, tribes entered Islam in waves, and the conquest of Makkah came with a handful of casualties instead of a generation of war. Two years later the Muslims entered Makkah, ten thousand strong.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: The treaty everyone hated opened the doors of Arabia. Have you ever had a 'defeat' that was actually a door?

title: The Letters to the Rulers
subtitle: The letter that reached the Emperor of Rome
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the letters to the rulers
Sahih al-Bukhari 2941 — the letter to Heraclius

chapters.heading: From the Prophet of Mercy
chapters.body: After Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ began the last stage of the mission — writing to the rulers of the world. The letter to Heraclius, Emperor of Rome, survives in the Sahih: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the servant of Allah and His Messenger, to Heraclius the Great of Rome. Peace be upon those who follow guidance... I call you to Islam: become Muslim and you will be safe, and Allah will double your reward; but if you turn away, you bear the sins of the peasants' (Bukhari 2941). Heraclius did not convert — but the hadith of Abu Sufyan (Sahih al-Bukhari; number not re-checked here) records that he questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet ﷺ. Other kings answered differently: the Negus of Abyssinia, who had sheltered the emigrants, embraced Islam before he died; the governor of Egypt, al-Muqawqis, sent gifts and courtesy but not faith; the ruler of Persia tore the letter. Khaybar, a Jewish stronghold north of Madinah, was taken in the same year (a seerah report; the terms and aftermath are not told here because they were not checked).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ wrote 'become Muslim and you will be safe' to the most powerful men alive. What does that tell you about the mission — fear, or invitation?

title: The Conquest of Makkah
subtitle: Eight years after being driven out — he enters with his head bowed
sources: Qur'an 110 — 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4280 — Abu Sufyan sees the Muslim forces enter Makkah; the Prophet's ﷺ flag at al-Hajun
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the details of the day

chapters.heading: The Day of Mercy
chapters.body: A Qurayshi breach of the truce opened the door, and in Ramadan of the eighth year, ten thousand Muslims descended upon Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ entered with his head lowered on his mount — reciting Surah Al-Fath, tradition records, in gratitude and humility, not triumph. The idols of the Kaaba came down by his own hand; the city that had stoned him, starved his clan, tortured his companions, killed his uncle and slandered his wives — stood waiting for vengeance. The seerah reports record his words to Quraysh at the door of the Kaaba: 'Go, for you are free' (Ibn Ishaq; the wording was not checked here). The general amnesty (with a small number of named exceptions, according to the seerah) turned many hearts. Within days the Kaaba's courtyard, emptied of idols, overflowed with new Muslims praying. And Surah An-Nasr speaks of that victory: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, And you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, Then exalt [Him] with praise of your Lord and ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance' (110:1-3). The conquest of Makkah ended not with an execution but with a prayer of repentance.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: He entered the city that tried to kill him and said 'you are free.' Who in your life deserves amnesty you have the power to give?

title: Hunayn and Taif
subtitle: Victory at Hunayn, and a city that later came to Islam
sources: Qur'an 9:25-27 — 'Allah has already given you victory in many regions'
Reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the Prophet's ﷺ words to the Ansar after Hunayn (hadith numbers not re-checked in this build)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — 'I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone'

chapters.heading: The Spoils and the Sweetness
chapters.body: After Makkah came Hunayn, against the Hawazin with their families and herds behind them — a new army with new wealth, and the first shock of the battle was a near-rout until the Prophet ﷺ stood firm on his mule calling the fleeing ranks back (9:25-27). The spoils of Hunayn were the richest of the Prophet's ﷺ life, and he distributed them to the hearts he was still winning — the new Makkan elite — until the Ansar, who had carried the faith in its hungriest years, murmured: he has given Quraysh and left us. He called them and said the words that settled their hearts and built their legend: are you not pleased that the people go home with sheep and camels, and you go home with the Messenger of Allah? — and they wept and said: yes, we are pleased with the Messenger of Allah (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Then the Prophet ﷺ marched to Taif, whose people had once turned him away; the siege was lifted without the city falling, and the people of Taif later sent a delegation and accepted Islam (seerah reports; details not checked here). The hope he voiced long before — that Allah would bring from their descendants people who would worship Allah alone — is recorded in Bukhari 3231.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Ansar were offered 'the Messenger of Allah' instead of wealth — and wept with joy. What would you take in place of money?

title: Tabuk
subtitle: The hardest march — and the hypocrites unmasked
sources: Qur'an 9:38-59 — the whole passage of the expedition
Qur'an 9:117-118 — 'Then He turned to them so they could repent'

chapters.heading: The Expedition of Hardship
chapters.body: In the heat of the ripening fruit season, news came that the Byzantines were massing at the northern border — and the Prophet ﷺ called the Muslims to the hardest expedition of his life: Tabuk, in the scorching end of summer, with the orchards heavy and the harvest calling. The hypocrites stayed behind with excuses, and the Qur'an unmasked them permanently in Surah At-Tawbah: 'If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people' (9:39). Three believers who stayed behind without excuse — Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions — were boycotted by the entire city, by order of the Prophet ﷺ, for fifty days, until the revelation came down forgiving them: 'the three who were left behind [and regretted their error] to the point that the earth closed in on them ... Then He turned to them so they could repent' (9:118). Tabuk was the last expedition of the Prophet's ﷺ life, and its lesson stands at the summit of the seerah: the community is measured not by the battles it wins but by the accountability it survives — even its greatest men were disciplined publicly, and even their repentance was written into the Qur'an for all time.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Ka'b ibn Malik's punishment became a verse of forgiveness. What mistake of yours could become your testimony?

title: The Farewell Sermon
subtitle: One speech, one standing — the charter of every Muslim generation
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 67 — the Prophet's ﷺ sermon on the sanctity of lives, wealth and honor
Sahih Muslim 1218 — Jabir's account of the Prophet's ﷺ Hajj and the Farewell address

chapters.heading: Listen Well, for I May Not Meet You Again Here
chapters.body: In the tenth year, the Prophet ﷺ performed his only full pilgrimage, and at Arafat, standing on his camel, he delivered the sermon that is the constitution of the ummah. The tradition preserves it: every Muslim's blood, property, and honor are inviolable, like this day, in this month, in this city; no usury from this day; no blood feud from this day; women have rights over you as you have rights over them; your brother's blood and property are sacred (Bukhari 67, Muslim 1218). Then he asked: have I conveyed? — and the valley answered: yes. And he raised his finger to the sky and said: O Allah, bear witness; O Allah, bear witness. And he told them, while he still stood before them healthy: those who are present must convey it to those who are absent — and he would be with them for only a few months more. The sermon of Arafat is remembered because it gathers, in one address, the dignity of life, wealth and honor.

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ said your brother's blood and property are sacred. Whose rights are you trampling right now without noticing?

title: The Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
subtitle: The house of Aisha, the sword of Umar, and the steadiness of Abu Bakr
sources: Qur'an 3:144 — 'if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]'

chapters.heading: Monday
chapters.body: The fever came in Safar of the eleventh year, after the farewell pilgrimage. For days the Prophet ﷺ grew weaker in the house of Aisha, sometimes joining the prayers seated, then directing Abu Bakr to lead the community in his place (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; numbers not re-checked here) — a command the early Muslims later recalled when Abu Bakr was chosen as leader. On Monday, with his head in Aisha's lap, he raised his eyes and said: rather, the Highest Companion (Aisha's account, reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; numbers not re-checked here) — and the greatest life in history ended with a choice: the prayer, or the Companion above. Umar stood and refused to believe it: he has not died; he has gone to his Lord as Musa went (Sahih al-Bukhari; number not re-checked here). Abu Bakr came from his house at al-Sunh, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed his forehead, and said: may my father and mother be sacrificed for you; by Allah, Allah will never cause you to die twice — then he recited the verse that had descended at Uhud for exactly this hour: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him' (3:144). The mosque of Madinah filled with weeping; the question of leadership was settled at the porch of Banu Sa'ida; and the man who had entered every city as a stranger left the world in the room of the wife he loved most, among his family, on his own bed, at peace. The tradition records that the day was Monday — the day of his birth.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Umar denied it; Abu Bakr recited Qur'an. When grief hits your family, which one will you be?

title: What He Left
subtitle: No palace, no hoard, no empire in his name — and an ummah that outlives empires
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2739 — the Prophet ﷺ left no money, only his mule, his weapons and a charitable land endowment
Sahih al-Bukhari 3092 — 'what we leave is charity'

chapters.heading: The Inventory of a Prophet
chapters.body: He died owning a mended cloak, a couch of palm-fiber that left marks on his side, a handful of barley, and a debt — his shield was still in pawn to a Jew of Madinah for the food of his household (the estate he left: Sahih al-Bukhari 2739; the cloak, the couch and the pawned shield are reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). A report preserves his last counsel as: the prayer, and those in your charge (collection and number not checked here). He left no son to inherit his authority and no fortune to divide: 'We, the company of prophets, leave no inheritance; what we leave is charity' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3092). Within thirty years of his death, his companions ruled from Egypt and Syria to Persia; within a century, the languages of three continents recited his book; within fourteen centuries, his followers number well over a billion. He left no statue of himself — the tradition forbids his image — and so the world built no monument to Muhammad except the practice of his message. In words reported from him: 'I have only been sent to perfect noble character' (reported by Ahmad; the number was not verified).
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: He left no inheritance but character. What will your children inherit from you that money can't buy?

title: Reflections: The Man Who Walked Beside Us
subtitle: Thirty chapters, one walk — what it means to follow him ﷺ
sources: Musnad Ahmad — 'I have only been sent to perfect noble character' (number not verified)
Sahih Muslim 45 — none of you truly believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself
Qur'an 33:21 — 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often'

chapters.heading: The Example
chapters.body: The Qur'an does not say the Prophet ﷺ was perfect so you could worship him. It says: 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often' (33:21) — what the Arabic calls uswa hasana. An example is for following. He was an orphan, so the orphan is honored. He was a merchant, so the scale is straight. He was driven from his city, so the stranger is sheltered. He was stoned, so the wounded are comforted. He conquered, so the conquered are forgiven. He ruled, so rulers are accountable. He died poor, so the poor are honored. Thirty chapters walked past like thirty footsteps — and the invitation of every one of them is the same: walk here. Not in his century, but in his character. One way to answer the question — what did he leave us? — is: nothing you can hold, and everything you can become.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Thirty chapters end here. Which single habit of his ﷺ — honesty, gentleness, patience, courage, mercy — will your family practice together this week?

title: Iqra — The First Word
subtitle: The first word of the final message was not 'believe' or 'obey' — it was 'read'
sources: Qur'an 96:1-5

chapters.heading: A Cave, a Covering, a Voice
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ had taken to the cave of Hira, seeking quiet from a city that troubled him. In Ramadan, at forty, the angel came to him, pressed him, and said one word: Iqra — the bundled Saheeh International text begins the verse 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created' (96:1). The man who would be called unlettered received a command built on the written word. Whatever else the world would say about this religion, its first word was an act of the mind.

chapters.heading: The Name of Your Lord
chapters.body: The reply to 'I cannot read' was not a scolding. It was the material itself: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Created man from a clinging substance. Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous - Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). Name first, then knowledge. Every act of learning in this deen begins with whose name is on it.

chapters.heading: What the First Word Decided
chapters.body: Notice what the first revelation did not say. Not 'rule', not 'conquer', not 'gather followers'. Read, in the name of your Lord. The command that launched a civilization made literacy an act of worship and inquiry a form of devotion. The Prophet ﷺ came home trembling, and Khadijah held him and said what the moment required: 'Allah will never disgrace you — you keep kinship, you carry the weak.' The first word chose knowledge; the first home chose comfort. The message has lived in both ever since.

familyQuestion: What are we 'reading' in our home this month — and in whose name do we begin?
